It also finds that the superior performance on English, even when not a source language, does not come with better alignment with human rationales.
papers.key_findings:
Models generally perform well on the languages they are trained on and align best with human rationales in these languages.
Performance is higher on English even when it is not a source language, but this performance is not accompanied by higher alignment with human rationales.
Multilingual models are not equally right for the right reasons across languages; Danish consistently shows the lowest alignment.
SHAP has higher agreement with human span rationales, while LIME has slightly higher agreement with human rank rationales.
Accuracy is only weakly correlated with alignment with human rationales, indicating multiple possible prediction strategies.
papers.limitation:
The languages chosen belong to the Indo-European language family, lacking linguistic diversity.
The multilingual parallel corpus of rationales is limited in size (250 annotations per language).
The language models are fine-tuned on translations, which may contain errors despite post-correction.
future_direction: Building larger rationale datasets for less related languages, including languages from different language families.
Further progress on multilingual interpretation and collection of rationales in different languages.
papers.abstract: Multilingual NLP models provide potential solutions to the digital language divide, i.e., cross-language performance disparities. Early analyses of such models have indicated good performance across training languages and good generalization to unseen, related languages. This work examines whether, between related languages, multilingual models are equally right for the right reasons, i.e., if interpretability methods reveal that the models put emphasis on the same words as humans. To this end, we provide a new trilingual, parallel corpus of rationale annotations for English, Danish, and Italian sentiment analysis models and use it to benchmark models and interpretability methods. We propose rank-biased overlap as a better metric for comparing input token attributions to human rationale annotations. Our results show: (i) models generally perform well on the languages they are trained on, and align best with human rationales in these languages; (ii) performance is higher on English, even when not a source language, but this performance is not accompanied by higher alignment with human rationales, which suggests that language models favor English, but do not facilitate successful transfer of rationales.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form during a training phase change that coincides with a dramatic improvement in in-context learning.
Architectural perturbations that shift induction head formation also shift in-context learning improvements accordingly.
Ablating induction heads in small models significantly reduces in-context learning ability.
Induction heads can implement abstract behaviors like translation and pattern matching, suggesting generality beyond literal copying.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models is plausible for general in-context learning, and behaviors are continuous from small to large models.
papers.limitation: Evidence is preliminary and indirect, especially for large models, with potential confounds or alternative hypotheses.
future_direction: Future work could build on these results to establish the claim more firmly.
Studying phase changes up close may offer generalizable lessons for safety in machine learning systems.
papers.abstract: Do induction heads constitute the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer language models? This blog presents indirect evidence that induction heads, circuits in transformers that copy and complete patterns, may be the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models. The evidence suggests induction heads likely play a major role in in-context learning, though for large models the case is correlational and not conclusive.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Painless Activation Steering: An Automated, Lightweight Approach for Post-Training Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do there exist activation steering (AS) methods that are both human-independent and adaptive to arbitrary models and arbitrary tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated, human-independent methods for activation steering that works with any labeled dataset, removing the need for manual prompt construction or feature annotation.
papers.conclusion: PAS provides a fast, lightweight, and practical automated option for post-training large language models, complementing weight- and prompt-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
PAS reliably improves performance on behavior tasks (bias, morality, alignment) but provides little benefit on intelligence-oriented tasks.
Introspective PAS variants (iPAS) perform best by constructing steering vectors from a model's own errors.
PAS complements existing methods, providing additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and outperforming Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on TruthfulQA.
PAS generally does not cause catastrophic forgetting on control tasks, except at very high steering strengths.
PAS is effective even in small data regimes and is computationally and storage efficient compared to weight-based methods.
papers.limitation:
PAS is ineffective on intelligence-oriented tasks that require specialized knowledge or advanced reasoning capacity.
At very high steering strengths, PAS can cause catastrophic forgetting on tasks like Sycophancy and TruthfulQA.
PAS is mathematically equivalent to modifying a single bias vector, which may limit its expressivity compared to methods that update all weights.
future_direction: Extending PAS through multi-task multi-layer composition.
Exploring alternative extraction methods for steering vectors.
Investigating new use cases for the PAS framework.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are typically post-trained for desired capabilities and behaviors via weight-based or prompt-based steering, but the former is time-consuming and expensive, and the latter is not precisely controllable and often requires manual trial-and-error. While activation steering (AS) promises a cheap, fast, and controllable alternative to the two existing post-training methods, current AS techniques require hand-crafted prompt pairs or labor-intensive feature annotation, making them more inconvenient than the plug-and-play methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We introduce Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated methods that make AS readily usable with any given labeled dataset, with no need for prompt construction, feature labeling, or human intervention. We evaluate PAS on three open-weight models (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B, and Nous-Hermes-2) and 18 tasks; we find that PAS reliably improves performance for behavior tasks, but not for intelligence-oriented tasks. The introspective variant (iPAS) delivers the strongest causal steering effects (10.1% on Bias, 5.2% on Morality, and 34.8% on Alignment). We also show PAS delivers additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and SFT. PAS constructs a fast, lightweight activation vector that can be cheaply trained, easily stored, and activated at will. Our results provide a characterization of where AS helps, where it fails, and how to deploy it as a practical, automated LM post-training option.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: A Study of Cross-Lingual Ability and Language-specific Information in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What factors influence the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT, and does language-specific information exist in its representations?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies datasize and context window size as crucial factors for cross-lingual transferability in multilingual BERT, and introduces Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to manipulate language-specific information for unsupervised token translation and improved cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The cross-lingual ability of m-BERT is learned from longer dependency and requires a massive amount of data; language-specific information can be manipulated via simple shifts to improve cross-lingual transfer, opening a new direction for strengthening cross-lingual ability.
papers.key_findings:
With small pretraining data, BERT does not outperform non-contextualized embeddings in cross-lingual ability; with large data, BERT achieves superior cross-lingual alignment.
Breaking down long dependency (smaller window size) hurts cross-lingual ability when pretraining data is large, but helps when data is small.
Language-specific information exists in m-BERT representations and can be extracted via mean difference vectors.
Applying Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to hidden representations can control the output language of m-BERT, enabling unsupervised token translation.
Using MDS to shift representations improves cross-lingual transfer performance on XNLI for most languages, except those with high subword overlap with English.
papers.limitation:
MDS does not improve performance for languages with high subword overlap with English (e.g., Spanish, French) due to shared subwords having different meanings, indicating the need for a more delicate mechanism.
The quality of unsupervised translation using MDS is not acceptable; only token conversion rate is measured, not fluency or accuracy.
future_direction: Develop a more delicate mechanism for applying language-specific shifts that considers differences among vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Recently, multilingual BERT works remarkably well on cross-lingual transfer tasks, superior to static non-contextualized word embeddings. In this work, we provide an in-depth experimental study to supplement the existing literature of cross-lingual ability. We compare the cross-lingual ability of non-contextualized and contextualized representation model with the same data. We found that datasize and context window size are crucial factors to the transferability. We also observe the language-specific information in multilingual BERT. By manipulating the latent representations, we can control the output languages of multilingual BERT, and achieve unsupervised token translation. We further show that based on the observation, there is a computationally cheap but effective approach to improve the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT.

papers.title: Interpretable by AI Mother Tongue: Native Symbolic Reasoning in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we construct a neural model that is both efficient and inherently interpretable by integrating discrete symbol learning with dynamic computational path selection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel hybrid Transformer architecture (Dynamic Intuition Classifier) that integrates a VQ-AIM encoder, symbolic router, and intuition gate to learn discrete, interpretable symbols and a two-phase training strategy with explainability-oriented loss functions, achieving competitive accuracy with transparent reasoning traces.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully embeds interpretability into the model's architecture through discrete symbols and gating, providing a step towards trustworthy AI by making the decision process transparent and traceable.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model achieves competitive classification accuracy on the AG News dataset while providing verifiable reasoning traces.
The gated fine-tuning strategy effectively enhances the purity of learned symbols and the sparsity of decisions.
The model's internal decision process, including intuition symbols and gating confidence, is transparent and traceable, enabling detailed analysis.
The two-phase, two-step training framework (Iterative Refinement Training) successfully cultivates a model with specialized intuitive capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are primarily conducted on a news classification dataset (AG News), which is relatively domain-specific, limiting the verification of generalizability to more diverse and complex NLP tasks.
Hyperparameters such as purity_lambda and gated_focus_lambda were set manually, which might limit the model's optimal performance.
future_direction: Model scaling by increasing d_model or codebook_size for more complex tasks.
Architectural evolution by introducing a Hierarchical Quantized VAE (HQ-VAE) for hierarchical semantic understanding.
Applying the architecture to other, more complex NLP tasks such as sequence labeling or text summarization.
Exploring automated hyperparameter tuning methods for weights like λpurity and λfocus.
Developing more advanced visualization tools, such as dynamically generating semantic descriptions for symbols.
papers.abstract: We present a framework where neural models develop an AI Mother Tongue, a native symbolic language that simultaneously supports intuitive reasoning, compositional symbol chains, and inherent interpretability. Unlike post-hoc explanation methods, our approach embeds reasoning directly into the model's representations: symbols capture meaningful semantic patterns, chains trace decision paths, and gated induction mechanisms guide selective focus, yielding transparent yet flexible reasoning. We introduce complementary training objectives to enhance symbol purity and decision sparsity, and employ a sequential specialization strategy to first build broad symbolic competence and then refine intuitive judgments. Experiments on AI tasks demonstrate competitive accuracy alongside verifiable reasoning traces, showing that AI Mother Tongue can serve as a unified mechanism for interpretability, intuition, and symbolic reasoning in neural models.

papers.title: What Do Llamas Really Think? Revealing Preference Biases in Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new logistic Bradley-Terry probe for detecting implicit association bias in LLM representations, and uses it to reveal substantial sociodemographic biases in the embeddings of various LLMs, showing that instruction fine-tuning does not eliminate these latent biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel method for assessing implicit preference bias in LLM representations and concludes that instruction fine-tuning insufficiently removes latent bias, extending previous findings on shallow word embeddings to contextualized embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed logistic Bradley-Terry probe outperforms WEAT and max-margin classification by a relative 27-34% in error rate on preference prediction tasks.
Middle layers of the LLMs yield the best probes for preference detection.
LLMs exhibit implicit biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender, favoring Western over Eastern countries, left-wing over right-wing ideologies, Christianity and Judaism over Islam, and female-prefixed careers over male-prefixed ones.
Instruction fine-tuning does not remove bias from the contextualized embeddings of LLMs.
CodeLLaMA models show less bias, likely due to additional pretraining on code.
future_direction: Thoroughly debias contextual word representations and reduce detectable bias.
Assess implicit bias in LLMs pretrained on different corpora and probe the effects of pretraining text choices on bias.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond? To bypass their refusal to "speak," we study this research question by probing contextualized embeddings and exploring whether this bias is encoded in its latent representations. We propose a logistic Bradley-Terry probe which predicts word pair preferences of LLMs from the words' hidden vectors. We first validate our probe on three pair preference tasks and thirteen LLMs, where we outperform the word embedding association test (WEAT), a standard approach in testing for implicit association, by a relative 27% in error rate. We also find that word pair preferences are best represented in the middle layers. Next, we transfer probes trained on harmless tasks (e.g., pick the larger number) to controversial ones (compare ethnicities) to examine biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender. We observe substantial bias for all target classes: for instance, the Mistral model implicitly prefers Europe to Africa, Christianity to Judaism, and left-wing to right-wing politics, despite declining to answer. This suggests that instruction fine-tuning does not necessarily debias contextualized embeddings. Our codebase is at https://github.com/castorini/biasprobe.

papers.title: Sparks of Rationality: Do Reasoning LLMs Align with Human Judgment and Choice?
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs exhibit human-like rational deliberation and emotion-driven biases in decision-making.
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning LLMs show higher compliance with rational choice axioms and are more sensitive to emotional steering, with in-context priming producing extreme shifts and representation-level steering yielding more human-like but less reliable effects.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a reproducible foundation for the scientific study of emotion, reasoning, and choice in LLMs, with implications for auditing and shaping LLM decision-making in real deployments.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking LLMs consistently elicit higher levels of rationality compared to non-thinking models.
In the absence of explicit task instructions, thinking models default to maximizing expected gains as prescribed by Expected Utility Theory.
Thinking models are more faithful at reproducing emotion-linked behavioral shifts directionally aligned with humans.
In-context priming induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate.
Representation-level steering produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability.
papers.limitation:
In-context priming induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate.
Representation-level steering produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly positioned as decision engines for hiring, healthcare, and economic judgment, yet real-world human judgment reflects a balance between rational deliberation and emotion-driven bias. If LLMs are to participate in high-stakes decisions or serve as models of human behavior, it is critical to assess whether they exhibit analogous patterns of (ir)rationalities and biases. To this end, we evaluate multiple LLM families on (i) benchmarks testing core axioms of rational choice and (ii) classic decision domains from behavioral economics and social norms where emotions are known to shape judgment and choice. Across settings, we show that deliberate "thinking" reliably improves rationality and pushes models toward expected-value maximization. To probe human-like affective distortions and their interaction with reasoning, we use two emotion-steering methods: in-context priming (ICP) and representation-level steering (RLS). ICP induces strong directional shifts that are often extreme and difficult to calibrate, whereas RLS produces more psychologically plausible patterns but with lower reliability. Our results suggest that the same mechanisms that improve rationality also amplify sensitivity to affective interventions, and that different steering methods trade off controllability against human-aligned behavior. Overall, this points to a tension between reasoning and affective steering, with implications for both human simulation and the safe deployment of LLM-based decision systems.

papers.title: Discriminating Form and Meaning in Multilingual Models with Minimal-Pair ABX Tasks
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning), and how do these representations evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free ABX-style discrimination framework for analyzing multilingual representations, and shows that in XLM-R, language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers over training, while meaning discrimination increases and stabilizes in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: ABX discrimination metrics provide a lightweight, interpretable tool for analyzing multilingual representations, revealing that language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers while meaning discrimination increases in deeper layers, with implications for understanding cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers.
Meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers.
There is a negative correlation between language and meaning discrimination across language pairs and checkpoints.
Language discrimination negatively correlates with performance on form-sensitive tasks like POS and NER in cross-lingual transfer.
Meaning discrimination does not consistently predict downstream task performance.
papers.limitation:
Encoder architecture and single-model scope: only tested on XLM-R (encoder-only), not decoder-only or encoder-decoder models.
Discrimination vs Separation: does not explicitly quantify separation in the representation space.
Task coverage: only POS, NER, NLI, may not capture deeper semantic capabilities.
Cross-linguistic generality vs. language-specific phenomena: not investigating specific languages or families in detail.
future_direction: Linking discrimination patterns to typological linguistic features.
Evaluating deeper semantic tasks.
Applying ABX metrics to decoder-only LLMs and more recent multilingual models.
papers.abstract: We introduce a set of training-free ABX-style discrimination tasks to evaluate how multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning). Inspired from speech processing, these zero-shot tasks measure whether minimal differences in representation can be reliably detected. This offers a flexible and interpretable alternative to probing. Applied to XLM-R (Conneau et al, 2020) across pretraining checkpoints and layers, we find that language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers, while meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers. We then explore probing tasks, showing some alignment between our metrics and linguistic learning performance. Our results position ABX tasks as a lightweight framework for analyzing the structure of multilingual representations.

papers.title: Large Reasoning Models Are (Not Yet) Multilingual Latent Reasoners
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks, often attributed to their capability to generate explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations. However, recent work shows that LRMs often arrive at the correct answer before completing these textual reasoning steps, indicating the presence of latent reasoning -- internal, non-verbal computation encoded in hidden states. While this phenomenon has been explored in English, its multilingual behavior remains largely unknown. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation of multilingual latent reasoning in LRMs across 11 languages. Using a truncation-based strategy, we examine how the correct answer emerges as the model is given only partial reasoning traces, allowing us to measure stepwise latent prediction formation. Our results reveal clear evidence of multilingual latent reasoning, though unevenly: strong in resource-rich languages, weaker in low-resource ones, and broadly less observable on harder benchmarks. To understand whether these differences reflect distinct internal mechanisms, we further perform representational analyses. Despite surface-level disparities, we find that the internal evolution of predictions is highly consistent across languages and broadly aligns with English -- a pattern suggesting an English-centered latent reasoning pathway.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Improving In-context Learning of Multilingual Generative Language Models with Cross-lingual Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual in-context learning and mitigate performance bias between languages in multilingual generative models using limited parallel data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a cross-lingual alignment framework (AFP) that uses multilingual contrastive learning and cross-lingual instruction following to improve cross-lingual abilities and reduce performance gaps in multilingual generative models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AFP framework improves cross-lingual capabilities and internal representations of multilingual generative models, reducing performance gaps between languages.
papers.key_findings:
AFP significantly improves cross-lingual in-context learning performance on various tasks with less than 0.1‰ of pre-training tokens.
AFP mitigates the internal representation gap between languages, leading to better-aligned and more uniform multilingual representations.
Cross-lingual instruction following (CIF) is more effective than multilingual instruction tuning (MIT) for cross-lingual ability.
AFP also improves performance on unseen languages for models like Llama that are pre-trained mainly on English.
The framework is effective across different model scales and architectures.
papers.limitation:
Relies on labeled parallel data, which is unavailable for languages without parallel samples.
Limited to models with up to 7.5B parameters due to computational constraints.
Error propagation from the machine translation system used may result in inferior performance.
future_direction: Extend the framework to align different modalities in multi-modal generative models.
Develop unsupervised multilingual alignment methods.
papers.abstract: Multilingual generative models obtain remarkable cross-lingual in-context learning capabilities through pre-training on large-scale corpora. However, they still exhibit a performance bias toward high-resource languages and learn isolated distributions of multilingual sentence representations, which may hinder knowledge transfer across languages. To bridge this gap, we propose a simple yet effective cross-lingual alignment framework exploiting pairs of translation sentences. It aligns the internal sentence representations across different languages via multilingual contrastive learning and aligns outputs by following cross-lingual instructions in the target language. Experimental results show that even with less than 0.1 {\textperthousand} of pre-training tokens, our alignment framework significantly boosts the cross-lingual abilities of generative language models and mitigates the performance gap. Further analyses reveal that it results in a better internal multilingual representation distribution of multilingual models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Identifying Cooperative Personalities in Multi-agent Contexts through Personality Steering with Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How do personality traits, steered via representation engineering, affect LLM behavior and cooperation in multi-agent games like the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma?
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering using representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, but with a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability to exploitation.
papers.conclusion: Personality steering through representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing a foundation for future work in cooperative AI agents.
papers.key_findings:
Steering towards agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness reduces troublemaking rates to zero.
High agreeableness increases exploitability, highlighting a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness lower lying rates, promoting honesty regardless of opponent behavior.
Models steered towards agreeableness and conscientiousness achieve better collective outcomes but worse individual outcomes.
Personality-steered behavior aligns with human psychological traits in similar contexts.
papers.limitation:
Limited to Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma variants and a single payoff matrix.
Effectiveness across different LLM architectures and tasks remains an open question.
Real-world multi-agent interactions involve more complex incentives.
future_direction: Explore diverse game-theoretic frameworks beyond IPD
Validate results across broader contexts and applications
Investigate effectiveness across different LLM architectures
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain autonomous capabilities, their coordination in multi-agent settings becomes increasingly important. However, they often struggle with cooperation, leading to suboptimal outcomes. Inspired by Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) tournaments, we explore how personality traits influence LLM cooperation. Using representation engineering, we steer Big Five traits (e.g., Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) in LLMs and analyze their impact on IPD decision-making. Our results show that higher Agreeableness and Conscientiousness improve cooperation but increase susceptibility to exploitation, highlighting both the potential and limitations of personality-based steering for aligning AI agents.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Uncovering Constraint-Based Behavior in Neural Models via Targeted\n Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does competition between linguistic constraints obscure underlying linguistic knowledge in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning re-weight constraints to uncover such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Models need to learn both linguistic constraints and their relative ranking; targeted fine-tuning can re-weight constraints to uncover dormant linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Mismatches between model and human linguistic behavior arise from either failure to learn constraints or failure to learn their ranking; targeted fine-tuning can help understand and adjust constraint rankings.
papers.key_findings:
English and Chinese models show an implicit causality (IC) bias, but Spanish and Italian models do not, due to competition with the pro-drop constraint.
Targeted fine-tuning demoting pro-drop in Spanish and Italian uncovers underlying IC knowledge.
Targeted fine-tuning promoting pro-drop in English and Chinese diminishes the IC bias.
Models learn linguistic constraints but may rank them incorrectly, leading to non-human-like behavior.
The failure to exhibit human-like behavior can be due to either not learning a constraint or not learning the correct constraint ranking.
future_direction: Pair behavioral analyses with representational probing to link model representations and behavior.
Explore constraint competition in different models like GPT-2.
Investigate other linguistic phenomena and constraints.
papers.abstract:
A growing body of literature has focused on detailing the linguistic
knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Existing work has
shown that non-linguistic biases in models can drive model behavior away from
linguistic generalizations. We hypothesized that competing linguistic processes
within a language, rather than just non-linguistic model biases, could obscure
underlying linguistic knowledge. We tested this claim by exploring a single
phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. While
human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, we find
cross-linguistic variation in model behavior. We show that competing processes
in a language act as constraints on model behavior and demonstrate that
targeted fine-tuning can re-weight the learned constraints, uncovering
otherwise dormant linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that
models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their
relative ranking, with mismatches in either producing non-human-like behavior.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
